title: Bootstrapping MLLM for Weakly-Supervised Class-Agnostic Object Counting
one_liner: A visual model learns to count any object type using only image-level counts instead of marking each object, by breaking counting into simpler dialogue steps and fusing local and global predictions.
lead: Object counting (estimating how many of something appear in an image) normally requires laboriously marking every single object by hand. This paper shows how a visual model can learn to count from much weaker labels: just the total count per image, not the location of each object. It works by asking the model to think aloud through dialogue, rank images by their counts, and combine nearby and full-image counting strategies.

problem.h2: Counting costs too much to annotate
paras: To teach a model to count, you normally point at each object in every training image. For a photo with fifty people, that is fifty clicks. For datasets with millions of images, this is months of human labor.

A beginner might hope to teach a model by just showing it images and their counts (fifty people in this photo, thirty in that one), without marking each one. The model should infer how many is in the picture. But naive visual models struggle: they learn shortcuts like 'image brightness is linked to density' rather than learning to actually spot and tally objects. They fail on new datasets where the shortcut breaks.

callout.html: The paper teaches a visual model to count using only the image-level total count as supervision, not the location of each object.

panels.title: 3. Dialogue thinking
panels.caption: Model guesses ranges: is it 50-100? Narrows down via multi-turn chat.

panels.title: 5. Any object, any count

steps.text: Model asks is the count 0-50 or 50-100? Narrows range each round.
Train model to rank image pairs: if image A has more objects, rank it higher.
Split image into overlapping tiles, count objects in each.
Estimate count from entire image at once.
Average or weight local tile predictions with global prediction for final count.

paras: Instead of adding point-level location labels (which is expensive), the paper changes how the model is trained: it uses three simple strategies that turn counting into easier sub-tasks, and trains the model to solve those instead.

hidden.h2: Counting confidence: what the model is really learning
hidden.name: relative-rank confidence
paras: The paper introduces a hidden quantity: how confident is the model that image A has more objects than image B? This is not the count itself, but a ranking signal (A > B, B > C). Training on this ranking is easier than predicting the exact number, because it forces the model to extract the visual features that actually distinguish high-density from low-density regions.

The paper measures this by comparing predictions on image pairs: when the model sees two images, does it correctly say which one is denser? That accuracy is the hidden ranking-confidence score. In the dialogue strategy, a hidden quantity is also the narrowing of the range each round: after each question, how much smaller is the remaining possibility? Tighter bounds mean higher confidence.

heat.caption: Darker means more constraining to the count; highlighted shows key comparisons that teach ranking.

reads.html: The model learns to say which image is denser by comparing them. Comparing is easier than predicting the exact count.

The compare-and-rank loss trains the model to maximize the margin between the count predictions for images with known relative ordering: if image A has more objects than image B, the model's A-count should exceed B-count by some amount.

mechanism.h2: Why the method works: three simpler puzzles instead of one hard one
paras: Predicting the exact count from weak labels is hard because the model must reverse-engineer the object locations from only a total number. Instead, the paper breaks it into three easier puzzles, and the model learns all three.

First, dialogue narrows the search space: asking 'is it 0-50?' is a yes/no question, much easier than guessing 47 exactly. Each round cuts the range in half, and the model gradually homes in. This works because the visual features that distinguish sparse from dense are learned in parallel.

Second, comparing images teaches the model what density looks like: if A has 80 objects and B has 20, the model must learn visual patterns of crowding. Ranking does not require the model to know the exact count, only which is more crowded. This is a simpler task than finding the exact number.

Third, local and global predictions are fused: some objects cluster in image corners (local detection catches them), while the full image gives context for overall density (global detection). Neither alone is perfect. Averaging them smooths out each predictor's mistakes because they fail in different places. A corner patch misses global trends, and a global view misses small clusters, but together they cover the blind spots.

stages.s: dialogue: narrow count range via binary questions
rank: learn which image is denser from pairs
local: count objects in image patches
fuse: average local and global predictions

math.words: penalty = compare-and-rank margin loss; for each pair of images with known ordering, penalize the model if it predicts the wrong rank order, weighted by how far the counts are in the pair
math.equation: L_rank = sum over (image_i, image_j) where count_i > count_j: max(0, margin - (pred_i - pred_j))
symbols: model's predicted count for image i
model's predicted count for image j
ground truth count for image i
minimum gap the model must achieve (e.g., 5 objects)
the ranking penalty for this pair

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Image A: true count 80, model predicts 75. Image B: true count 30, model predicts 40.
Since A has more objects (80 > 30), we require model prediction A > B, i.e., 75 > 40. This holds.
Margin = 5. Gap achieved = 75 - 40 = 35. Penalty = max(0, 5 - 35) = 0 (model did well).
Image C: true count 60, model predicts 55. Image D: true count 50, model predicts 58.
C should rank higher (60 > 50), but model says D > C (58 > 55). Wrong order.

math.note: The margin prevents lazy predictions; the model must confidently rank denser images higher, which forces it to learn real visual crowding cues.

bars.h2: Weak supervision vs. full supervision: counting accuracy

charts.title: Naive weak-only method
charts.note: Training on total count alone without dialogue, ranking, or fusion misses details and guesses poorly.

charts.title: WS-COC (this paper)
charts.note: Three strategies—dialogue, ranking, local-global fusion—align the model's visual reasoning with actual object locations, even without point labels.

items.b: Dialogue gets stuck at coarse ranges.
items.html: If the model's binary questions are poorly tuned (e.g., always asking 0-50 vs. 50-100), it does not refine well. Adaptive range selection is needed—the dialogue must adjust based on what earlier questions revealed.

items.b: Ranking signal is weak on similar images.
items.html: When two images have very similar object counts (78 vs. 80), the compare-and-rank loss gives little gradient—the model does not learn much from that pair because the gap is small. Training on diverse count ranges helps, because large gaps (e.g., 20 vs. 80) produce strong rank signals that teach the model clear crowding patterns.

If local patches cluster detection in one corner and global sees a uniform image, fusing them by averaging can yield a count between two wrong answers. Adaptive weighting (trust local in dense regions, global in sparse) is better than simple averaging because each method's strength complements the other: local detectors excel at tight clusters but miss spread-out objects, while global detectors catch overall density but blur fine structure. Weighting each by where it succeeds avoids the compromise of averaging two weak estimates.
Dialogue uses adaptive ranges; training pairs span low to high counts; local and global predictions are learned jointly so they complement rather than contradict.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo should start with a small image dataset where you know the true object counts (e.g., 20 images of scattered dots, with counts 5-95). Train the three-strategy model on only the image-level counts. Then measure: (1) can it rank image pairs by density correctly? (2) do the local and global count predictions agree roughly? (3) is the final fused count close to the true count? Plot the model's predicted counts against true counts; the points should lie near the diagonal, not scattered.
demo.metric_eq: ranking_accuracy = fraction of image pairs where model predicts higher count for the denser image; count_error = mean absolute difference between predicted and true counts
demo.closing: If ranking accuracy exceeds 90% and count error drops below 10% of the average count, the paper's strategy is working: the model learned to spot density without point labels.
